newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Analysts see further gains at Russia's Sberbank.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see further gains at Russia's Sberbank.

text.p: Shares in Russia's largest bank, Sberbank, which have become one of the most actively traded stocks in Moscow, are set to appreciate further, analysts said on Monday.
But they cautioned that the main growth spurt was over and said the retail bank needed flexibility to maximise potential.

The mostly state-owned Sberbank, whose assets total $31 billion, was transferred to the first level of the Russian Trading System late last month after its share price jumped almost 400 percent from around $30 last autumn to over $140 now.

Analysts predict shareholders are likely to see further gains as the bank, which holds a massive 104.3 trillion roubles in savings deposits, or 75 percent of total private savings, see more active trading on the liquid RTS.
A CentreInvest Securities report published early this year said the target value for the stock was $443. It did not give a time frame for the growth.
"It is truly a blue chip -- it gives the exposure to Russia's retail banking sector," said James Fenkner, director of research at CentreInvest Securities.

Sergei Komlev, a banking analyst at United Financial Group said each of Sberbank's approximately 34,000 branches was valued at only $60,000, or as much as a one-room Moscow flat, at the bank's current level of capitalisation.

"Even with the recent authorisations, it will be traded at less than two times its price/earnings ratio," he said, referring to a shareholder vote last week to raise paid-up capital from 700.1 billion roubles to one trillion roubles.
"Banks in Eastern Europe are traded at five to eight times the p/e ratio, while the biggest bank in Eastern Europe (Sberbank) is traded at less than two times."

Analysts said a change of management last year was beneficial, cutting out unprofitable branches and seeking to present a more open profile to the West, despite restrictions on share ownership, with plans to tap international markets soon.

"I think there's a lot of investor interest," said Jim Nail, head of research for Russia at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "If they come out with an internationally tradable instrument, I think they would definitely have a lot of interest."
Sberbank is also planning an international-standard audit.

Sberegatelny Bank Rossiiskoi Federatsii, or Sberbank, posted 14.5 trillion roubles pre-tax profit in 1996, up from 4.3 trillion roubles in 1995, and a 30,000 rouble dividend per ordinary share with a face value of 50,000 roubles.

But analysts said earnings and share appreciation would be slowed by recent low yields on the Treasury bill market, which Sberbank dominates with holdings of over 40 percent of all outstanding T-bills -- half its assets at the start of the year.
The annualised average yield on treasury bills is currently around 25 percent, down from about 60 percent last year.
"We don't expect (the stock price) to rocket," said Fenkner. "It will be a core stock, it's a good long term stock to get into, but it has already had its initial trajectory."
Analysts said diversification of the bank's activities would be central to its continuing success.
"They're at a crucial point in their operations, and it is going to be very important how they adapt to the lower GKO (Treasury bill) yields," said Nail.
"The real question operationally is: will they be able to convert their business to find new areas of opportunity?"
The Central Bank owns a controlling stake of 50 percent plus one share in Sberbank, whose other major shareholders include Tokobank and Vneshtorgbank Rossii.
